title: Is Divorce Ever Right, and May a Divorced Person Remarry?
excerpt: Jesus and Paul speak about divorce in five passages, and Christians who honor every one of them give three different answers about when a marriage may end and whether another may follow. All three agree on what to say to a person who is in danger.
body:
Three people have the same page of the Bible open. One is a man whose wife left him six years ago. He has met someone, and he can't tell whether Jesus would call the wedding he is planning a marriage or adultery. One is the pastor he has asked to perform it, who has read four books on the subject and found four answers. And one is a woman who is afraid of the man she lives with, and who has been told by people she trusts that God hates divorce.

A skeptic looking over their shoulders has a fair complaint. Either Jesus meant what he said about divorce, in which case most churches ignore him, or he didn't, in which case the words are being used only when someone wants a weapon. And he will point out that the weapon has mostly been used on women.

Much of that is true, and the woman's case comes before the other two. If you are in danger, get safe first and sort the theology after. The Find Help page on this site is a place to start. It is here: [Find Help](/help). If you're in immediate danger, call 911.

An earlier essay on this site sets out [the rabbis' debate that Jesus walked into and the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readings of his answer](/writing/divorce-remarriage-and-the-church). This one takes the two questions in its title. It reads the five passages one at a time, and then sets out the three answers Christians give.

## Five Passages

In Mark the question is put to Jesus in the territory of Herod Antipas, who had executed John the Baptist for condemning his marriage to his brother's wife. It was a dangerous question in that place. Jesus answers from creation, as he does in Matthew: "What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate" (Mark 10:9). Afterward, in the house, he tells the disciples, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery" (Mark 10:11–12). There is no exception. The sin he names is divorcing and marrying another, the two acts together. And he applies it to wives as well as husbands, which fitted a Roman world where either spouse could end a marriage.

Luke has one sentence, with no setting and no exception: "Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery" (Luke 16:18).

In the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew 5, the saying has a different shape. "Everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery" (Matthew 5:32). The weight falls on the husband. In a world where a dismissed wife often had to marry again in order to live, the man who sends her away without cause is held responsible for what follows.

In Matthew 19 the Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife "for any cause" (Matthew 19:3), a phrase only Matthew records. Jesus says that Moses allowed divorce "because of your hardness of heart," and then: "whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery" (Matthew 19:8–9). The disciples are shocked enough to say that "it is better not to marry" (Matthew 19:10), and he doesn't take it back. "Not everyone can receive this saying" (Matthew 19:11).

Two things in that sentence have been argued over ever since. The first is the word translated "sexual immorality." It is a broad word. The Study Bible's notes on this site list four readings of it: adultery, sexual sin of any kind, unfaithfulness discovered during a betrothal, as when Joseph "resolved to divorce her quietly" (Matthew 1:19), and marriage within the degrees of kinship that Leviticus forbids. The second is how far the exception reaches. It plainly qualifies the divorcing. Whether it also qualifies "and marries another" is what the first two answers below disagree about.

In 1 Corinthians 7 Paul separates what he has from Jesus from what he adds himself. From the Lord: "the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife" (1 Corinthians 7:10–11). The words in the middle matter. Paul knows of a wife who has already left. He doesn't order her back. He gives her two paths, and marrying someone else is neither of them.

Then, "I, not the Lord," he takes up a case Jesus was never asked about, a believer married to an unbeliever. The believer should stay. "But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15). He doesn't say what the believer is freed from. Later in the chapter he writes, "Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned" (1 Corinthians 7:27–28), and readers differ over whether the people he calls free include the divorced or only those who have never married. He ends the chapter with the rule he began from: "A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives" (1 Corinthians 7:39).

The skeptic has a question about these five, and it is a reasonable one. Three of them give no exception and Matthew gives one twice. Some scholars conclude that Jesus forbade divorce outright and that Matthew's church softened a demand it found too hard. Others answer that ancient writers regularly shortened a teacher's words, and that Mark and Luke give the rule while Matthew gives the rule with its qualification. The texts don't settle which, and each of the answers below has to live with that.

On some points the five passages agree, and nobody disputes them. Marriage is meant for life. Divorce is always counted a loss. The person who ends a marriage in order to marry someone else is called an adulterer. The passages leave three things open: what the exception in Matthew covers, whether it frees anyone to marry again, and what "not enslaved" means. Under those lies a larger question. Were Jesus and Paul giving a complete list of grounds, or answering the particular questions that were put to them?

## The First Answer: No Remarriage While a Spouse Lives

The oldest answer is that a husband or wife may have to separate from a spouse, but that neither may marry anyone else while the other lives. This was the common teaching of the early church, it remains the teaching of the Catholic Church in its own form, and a number of Protestants hold it.

Jerome stated it without cushioning in the 390s. He had been asked about a woman who left a husband guilty of gross sexual sin and then married another man. His reply grants that she had cause to leave. Then: "he may be stained with every crime and may have been left by his wife because of his sins; yet he is still her husband and, so long as he lives, she may not marry another."

In its holders' own terms the case runs like this. Mark, Luke and Paul record no exception. Paul's two paths for the separated wife are to stay unmarried or be reconciled. He says a wife is bound as long as her husband lives, and he says it again in Romans (Romans 7:2). Matthew's exception allows the sending away, or refers to betrothal or unlawful unions, and does not license a second marriage. They add that the disciples' dismay makes sense only on this reading. If Jesus had merely agreed with the stricter rabbis, nobody would have said it was better not to marry. Behind the texts stands a conviction about what marriage is. It pictures a covenant God does not break, and the spouse who waits keeps the way home open for the one who left.

The hard questions for this answer are real. Matthew gives the exception twice, and it has to mean something. The innocent partner is held for life to a bond the other has trampled. And the practice was never as uniform as the theory. Origen, a century and a half before Jerome, noted that "some even of the rulers of the church have permitted a woman to marry, even when her husband was living." He thought this contrary to Scripture. He also said it was done "not indeed altogether without reason."

## The Second Answer: Two Grounds

The second answer came with the Reformation. Erasmus argued in 1519 that the wronged husband or wife in Matthew's exception could take a new spouse. The Protestant churches adopted that reading and joined Paul's case to it. The Westminster Confession of 1646 names two grounds, adultery and willful desertion that can't be mended, and it holds that the wronged party in a divorce for adultery is as free to marry as if the other had died.

Their reasoning is that in the world of Jesus a valid divorce and the right to remarry were one thing. A certificate of divorce existed to say that the woman was free to marry. An exception to the rule against divorce is therefore an exception to the whole sentence. "Not enslaved" means not bound, they say, and a person no longer bound is free. On this view Jesus named one act that breaks the one-flesh union from inside, and Paul named another.

The people who wrote this answer down knew its danger. The same confession prefaces its two grounds with a warning about "the corruption of man" that is "apt to study arguments, unduly to put asunder those whom God hath joined together in marriage."

This answer too has hard questions. It has to account for Mark, for Luke, and for Paul's "remain unmarried or else be reconciled." And it is asked why the grounds number exactly two. If Paul could add a ground the Lord had not mentioned, then Jesus' sentence was not a closed list, and the question arises of what else might belong on it. In its strict form this answer has also had a gap. A wife whose husband is cruel to her, though he has neither been unfaithful nor moved out, was told that she could live apart from him but could never be free.

## The Third Answer: Wider Grounds, Including Abuse

The third answer starts from that gap. Many Protestant churches now teach that abuse and hard-hearted abandonment of a spouse's most basic needs break the marriage covenant as truly as adultery does.

In its holders' terms, Jesus was asked about divorce "for any cause" and rejected it. He was refusing the groundless dismissal of wives. He wasn't reciting every ground the Scriptures know. The law he and his hearers shared had long protected a wife's claim to "her food, her clothing," and "her marital rights," and said that if a husband withheld them, "she shall go out for nothing" (Exodus 21:10–11). That law concerns a wife taken from among slaves, and the argument is that a free wife cannot have had less protection than she did. Paul's phrase is given its plain force: a believer whose spouse has made the marriage a place of terror is "not enslaved," and God has called her to peace. On this view the man who beats his wife has deserted the marriage without leaving the house. He has broken the covenant, and she has done no wrong by saying so.

The hard questions are these. Neither Jesus nor Paul names abuse as a ground, and the Exodus law stands a long way from 1 Corinthians. Once the list is opened, it is hard to say where it closes. Cruelty shades into unkindness and neglect into disappointment, and Westminster's warning about studied arguments was written for moments like that. Holders of the first answer say that this is the "any cause" divorce coming back under a better name. Holders of the third reply that a rule which can't tell a violent home from a dull one has failed in a way that is worse.

## What No Passage Says

One thing is not in dispute among the three, and it has to be said plainly because it has so often been left unsaid. None of these passages tells you to stay in danger. The Study Bible's note on Matthew 19, on this site, puts it this way: "Jesus' words never require anyone to remain where they or their children are in danger; separation for safety is not what this text condemns."

The strictest writers agree. Jerome allows that the woman in his letter had reason to go. Paul's own sentence allows for a wife who has left. The Catholic Church, which holds that the bond cannot be dissolved, teaches that spouses may live apart for serious cause. The three answers disagree about whether the marriage can be ended and whether another may follow. On whether a person may leave a house where someone is hurting them, there is no disagreement to report. A pastor who sends anyone back into danger with these verses has added to them.

Scripture does not treat getting away from violence as a failure of faith. David went out through a window the night Saul's men came for him, and it was his wife who told him to go (1 Samuel 19:11–12). Paul was lowered over the wall of Damascus in a basket (Acts 9:25). When a crowd picked up stones, "Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple" (John 8:59). The psalmist says of God that "his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence" (Psalm 11:5).

Leaving safely can take planning and help. Nothing here is legal advice, and a page is no substitute for people who know your situation. If you need someone sooner, [Find Help](/help) lists hotlines for abuse and sexual assault.

## What We Have Done With the Three Answers

We have tended to hold whichever answer suited the case in front of us. We have been strict about other people's marriages and understanding about our own, or our children's. We have used the first answer to keep women beside men who hurt them, and called it faithfulness to the words of Jesus. We have used the third to approve the ending of marriages that were only hard, and called it compassion. And we have let the divorced sit at the back for decades, as though the one sin Jesus forgave slowly were theirs.

If you are grieving a marriage that ended, you are not a second-class Christian. Grace is not the reward for a clean history.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess together that God made marriage and meant it for life, that breaking it is a grave thing whoever does the breaking, that adultery, desertion and violence against a spouse are sins, and that there is forgiveness in Christ for everyone who has failed here. Seeking safety is not a sin on any reading.

Whether a divorce can be right, on what grounds, and whether a divorced person may marry again while a former spouse lives, are questions of the second order. Faithful churches give the three answers above. This essay has set them side by side and does not choose among them, and it can't rule on anyone's marriage. That belongs to people who know the facts, in a church that has thought its position through.

So the man in the first paragraph still doesn't have his answer, and neither does his pastor. They have five passages, three careful readings, and a Lord whose disciples found his teaching on this hard enough that they wondered aloud whether anyone should marry at all. He let their dismay stand. Whatever the two of them decide, they will be deciding it in front of him. The woman is the only one of the three who has been told something certain. She can go.

*"What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."* (Mark 10:9)

*"He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds."* (Psalm 147:3)
